column10: [Half Year 2023 Metro Performance Glass Ltd Earnings Call AUCKLAND Dec 1, 2022 (Thomson StreetEvents) -- Edited Transcript of Metro Performance Glass Ltd earnings conference call or presentation Monday, November 28, 2022 at 9:00:00pm GMT TEXT version of Transcript ================================================================================ Corporate Participants ================================================================================ * Brent Mealings Metro Performance Glass Limited - CFO * Simon J. Mander Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO ================================================================================ Conference Call Participants ================================================================================ * Grant Lowe Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research ================================================================================ Presentation -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [1] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- My name is Simon Mander, and I'm the CEO of Metro Performance Glass, and with me is our CFO, Brent Mealings. This morning, we will provide you with an overview of the group's results for the 6 months to the 30th of September 2022, and we'll then be happy to take any questions. Turning now to Slide 2. We've noted 4 key messages which summarize the year. I'd like to start by noting challenging market conditions faced in the first half, particularly in New Zealand. We've been focused on our customers, recovering of our gross margins and preparing the business for the expected increase in Low E glass production as a result of introduced building code changes. The series of price increases we have introduced are beginning to show in our margins from the second quarter, and we expect this to continue through the second half. Australian Glass Group delivered on its turnaround plan achieving a significantly improved performance driven by solid demand and price increases. Our net debt has increased in the first half, primarily driven by an increase in working capital due to ongoing supply chain disruption, higher-value inventory and debtors. We also commenced a cost-out program, and I'll expand on this program with initiatives later in the session. Moving to our key financial results for the first half on Slide 3. Group EBITDA of $5.6 million was an increase of 78% on the prior comparable period, driven by a full trading period without a lockdown and significant price increases in both New Zealand and Australia. Net debt increased from the full year to $59.1 million, driven by working capital requirements. Our leverage ratio remains consistent with the full year result at 3.8x. During the period, Metroglass concluded an additional year extension on its current syndicated banking facilities out to the end of October 2024. On Slide 4, New Zealand revenue of $100 million was up 14% versus the previous comparable period with an EBIT of $3.6 million, down 15%. Q1 was a major contributor to the earnings impact in the first half with the additional price increases introduced in June and September, beginning to recover margins in the second quarter. All of our segments faced disruptions in supply chains, project delays and people availability challenges that impacted operational efficiency. In spite of this, all segments delivered improved results in the prior year, primarily driven by a full trading period and the price increases. Our focus on continually improving the customer experience continues to reflect the positive levels of customer satisfaction, achieving a 7.9 out of 10 in our latest survey in May 2022. Another key milestone is the installation of the new furnace of the Highbrook plant in Auckland, and this project has progressed very well and is undergoing its final commissioning phase now. On Slide 5, in light of the year-on-year decline in volumes and an expectation that further declines are likely later in the new calendar year, Metroglass is undertaking organizational review and implemented a series of initiatives across the group to ensure capacity and resources are appropriate to service demand as the cycle changes. Following recent investments in processing capability and furnace capacity at our Auckland and Christchurch plants, business is now in a position to rationalize its production footprint and we will cease manufacturing operations in the Bay of Plenty by the end of December 2022. Metroglass will continue to have sales recommendation, commercial and residential blazing resources in a retrofit presence in the important Bay of Plenty market. The overall cost out program, including the Bay of Plenty site rationalization is expected to achieve annualized savings in the New Zealand business in the range of $8 million to $9 million, with benefits occurring from the second half of FY '23. Regrettably, these changes impact on a number of our people, and we are committed to supporting our impacted team through this period. On Slide 6, Australian Glass Group's revenue of $38.2 million was up 32% versus prior year with an EBIT of $2.6 million, up $3.3 million from the modest loss in the first half of FY '22. We're also pleased to see solid gross margins in that business. AGG delivered on its turnaround plan, achieving revenue and EBIT targets for first half '23, supported by stable operating performance and price increases. Also pleasing to see that New South Wales business has made a significant turnaround in the half. AGG now enters the next phase of its strategy, having achieved its turnaround and is well positioned for growth alongside the increasing adoption of double glazing and changes to the National Construction Code, NTC, coming into force in 2023 that will further accelerate its uptake. I'll now hand over to Brent to discuss the financial results in more detail. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Brent Mealings, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CFO [2] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thanks, Simon, and good morning, everyone. On Slide 7, we break our revenue down. And in New Zealand, you can see an overall increase of 14% as all segments achieved year-on-year improvements. As Simon has already mentioned, we are also happy to see continued improvement in the AGG business. Slide 8 reflects our half year results. Segmental results are on the right-hand side of the page. New Zealand's gross profit margin for the half was impacted by the increase in input costs prior to the scheduled price increases progressively introduced in Q1. In line with expectations, we have begun to see margin improve from Q2. In Australia, gross profit margin almost doubled, in part reflecting the price increase in response to cost inflation pressures, but also in recognition of the increasing value of Glass throughout the industry. Turning to the group results on the left-hand side of it, our net profit after tax increased from $400,000 to $600,000. I'd like to move to the waterfall on Slide 9. Movements in New Zealand's EBIT results are shown in gray shading. Our New Zealand EBIT result was $0.5 million lower than the prior year, with higher revenue offset by increased input costs that we were unable to offset by market price increases at the same rate. Increases in distribution and glazing were partly offset by savings elsewhere. Turning to the Australian performance, which is in the green shaded area of the waterfall. The encouraging story here is revenue growth and gross profit margin profit improvements. It has largely offset the inflationary cost pressures. ACT has achieved a solid turnaround in profitability in the half. Turning to the balance sheet slide, Slide 10. Net operating cash flows were significantly below the comparative period primarily driven by requirements on working capital. Capital expenditure has reduced to $5 million in the first half with a focus on targeted investments and maintenance checking only. On our big points on the slide, we have noted comparisons between the first half of 2022 and the full year 2022. I'd like to focus on comparisons to the full year ended 31st of March. Net debt has increased by $6.8 million since March, driven by the working capital requirements and inventory primarily with our leverage ratio consistent with March 22 at 3.8x net debt to EBITDA. Back to you, Simon. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [3] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thanks. Now turning now to the outlook for FY '23 on Slide 11. The number of residential consents in New Zealand has been running at elevated levels and well above the industry capacity, supporting a stable pipeline of work in the near term. However, we expect that economic headwinds are likely to reduce the number of dwellings actually constructed later in calendar year 2023. Updates to the H1 building code, applicable consents from November '22 will support an increased demand for higher-performing Low E glass, and this will have positive impact on gross profit performance. The overall cost-out program, including the Bay of Plenty site rationalization is expected to achieve annualized savings in the New Zealand business in the range of $8 million to $9 million with benefits accruing from the second half of FY '23. Any slowdown in Australian construction activity is likely to be offset by increases in the market penetration of double glazing and accelerated by the upcoming changes to the National Construction Code in 2023. We believe we are very well positioned to meet the requirements and opportunities for them to book the upcoming changes in the New Zealand and Australian building insulation regulation code changes. Finally, on Slide 12. The Metroglass' strategy and focus remain unchanged as we continue to build resilience and defend our leadership position in a competitive New Zealand market, grow profitability of our Australian business and benefit from increasing demand for double glazing to ensure our balance sheet is strong and sufficient to table future risks and opportunities. Now that brings us to the end of our presentation, and we're now happy to answer any questions that you may have. Thank you. ================================================================================ Questions and Answers -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [1] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (Operator Instructions) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [2] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- It's Grant Lowe from Jarden. Can you hear me okay? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [3] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [4] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Great. Just so looking at the geographical results, firstly, just in terms of New Zealand, I see gross margins were down $41.6 million versus $44.4 million in the first half last year. Can you give us a sense as to the split quarter-on-quarter, you filled out that the second quarter was an improvement on the first? Just trying to understand that momentum coming out into the second half. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [5] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. So as we sort of described, Grant, Q1 was difficult at a gross profit performance level given the timing of the price increases, which we start beginning of June and the beginning of March, and the one at the beginning of June was $11.75 million. So it was quite a decent increase. So what we've seen is from Q2 onwards, quite a good improvement in our gross profit and we're (inaudible) appearing into the second half. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [6] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. Is it reasonable to assume that it might be at around the 44% in the second half? Or is that (inaudible) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [7] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- What percentage did you say? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [8] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- If it was 44.4% in the first half last year. Is that a reasonable assumption going into the second half? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [9] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, I don't think that'd be too far off we would be aiming for. Yes. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [10] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. Excellent. And then in terms of Australia, just so I understand correctly positive result there, which is great. You've said that any slowdown in construction activity is likely to be increased, offset by increases in market penetration and changes and the like. Are we to sort of looking into at any major changes? Are we expecting that earnings might be able to remain at these levels going forward just by scope? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [11] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [12] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. Good sense. Around the debt side of things. I guess I was surprised to see that to go up by quite so much. In terms of, obviously, working capital driving that. In terms of -- we think that at the moment is working, our working capital levels sort of a reasonable go-forward basis? Or are there -- do you expect to see some unwind either in terms of inventory or receivables in particular? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Mander, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CEO [13] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The major driver of the -- apart from the price increases, which obviously have an impact, but the supply chain disruption is still an issue we're having to deal with in terms of our safety levels. We're holding something like 40% more inventory at the end of September compared to March. So to the extent that the supply chain disruption starts to settle down in the new year, we see that as an opportunity to wind that back, but it's been in the recent weeks, there's been -- you probably have seen the press around the New Zealand ports in particular. And this is probably a Christmas as well. So we're hopeful that beyond into the new year, we can find that out. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [14] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. Okay. So in terms of that 40% lift September versus March, is that in dollar values rather than volume? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Simon J. Is that still remain at $75 million facility? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Brent Mealings, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CFO [17] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The total facility is $80 million. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grant Lowe, Jarden Limited, Research Division - VP of Equity Research [18] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Including the arbitrage? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Brent Mealings, Metro Performance Glass Limited - CFO [19] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sorry, Grant. column10: [Half Year 2023 Kiwi Property Group Ltd Earnings Call Auckland Nov 29, 2022 (Thomson StreetEvents) -- Edited Transcript of Kiwi Property Group Ltd earnings conference call or presentation Sunday, November 27, 2022 at 9:00:00pm GMT TEXT version of Transcript ================================================================================ Corporate Participants ================================================================================ * Clive Mackenzie Kiwi Property Group Limited - CEO ================================================================================ Conference Call Participants ================================================================================ * Arie Dekker Jarden Securities Ltd - Managing Director * Nick Mar Macquerie Group Limited - Analyst * Bianca Fledderus UBS AG - Analyst ================================================================================ Presentation -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [1] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thank you for standing by. Welcome to Kiwi Property FY23 Interim Results Webcast. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. (Operator Instructions) Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today to Clive Mackenzie, CEO. Please go ahead. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Clive Mackenzie, Kiwi Property Group Limited - CEO [2] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thank you, [Dilem]. [Kia ore], everyone, and good morning, and thank you for joining us for Kiwi Property's interim results announcement for the six months ended 30 September 2022. I am Clive Mackenzie, the CEO of Kiwi Property. And today I'm joined by our CFO, Gavin Parker, and our Head of Investor Relations, [Cam Hodgetts]. Assume you all have a copy of our presentation in front of you. If not, you can access one from the Annual Results section of our website at kp.co.nz. A quick reminder that as usual, we have included detailed financial and property slide in the appendices to this document. I'll take the disclaimer as read, so please turn to slide five. As you all aware, we are operating in a challenging economic climate, high inflation, rising interest rates, and a labor supply shortage has created a significant uncertainty in the market. During this volatile period, the delivery of our strategy is more important than ever. Our evolution from a retail and office landlord to the creator of connected communities continues to gain momentum. While this transition will take time, as you will hear today, we sustained a robust operating performance over the past six months, while taking the business closer to our goal of becoming a developer, owner, and operator of mixed-use assets at key metropolitan centers and transport hubs. We believe that by intensifying our mixed-use assets, leveraging diverse capital sources, enabling the success of our customers, and driving operational excellence, we'll be in the strongest position to grow shareholders' returns. Kiwi Property's active leasing and asset management platforms are source of competitive advantage and have enabled us to maintain highly productive assets despite the impact of COVID-19. You will recall the consistent rental and sales growth delivered across our portfolio over recent periods. And we are proud to have maintained this positive trajectory. During the six months to 30 September, Kiwi Property earned a $100 million in net rental income, marking a new record for the company. Despite concerns about the macro-economic climate, we grew rents by an impressive 4.9%, while continuing to keep our high-quality asset portfolio almost fully occupied. Sales across our mixed-use and retail assets were up nearly 10% on the same time last year, with the Sylvia Park precinct alone generating more than $750 million in sales over the past 12 months. And importantly, we achieved all these milestones while continuing to improve the quality, resilience, and sustainability of our assets. Our focus on ESG was rewarded with the [GRESB] score of 81 for the year, placing us among some of Australasia's most successful reach. These figures are testament to the strength and resilience of our assets. As we've been saying for some time, flagship retail destinations are continuing to go from strength to strength even as second-tier assets come under pressure. Data released by NZ Post at the start of November showed that with Kiwis now settling into a post-pandemic norm, there's been a shift from online to in-store shopping. Online spending fell for the second quarter in a row and is now below where it was two years ago. At the same time, in-store spending is now 14% above pre-pandemic Q3 2019 levels. Discussions about the future retail often overlooked the fact that not all retail is the same and it shouldn't be viewed as such. We are proud to own and operate as some of New Zealand's best shopping destinations, putting us in the driver's seat to benefit from retail to clear bifurcation. We made significant progress on our targeted development program in the first half, bringing Sylvia Park's transformation into a world-class mixed-use community ever closer to fruition. Construction of the precinct's 295 built-to-rent apartment complex is moving forward at pace with the steel superstructure now up to three levels high in some places. This exciting project will help embed Kiwi Property as a leader in BTR in New Zealand and help us to capture the financial benefit that we believe will flow from the new asset class over time. Elsewhere at Sylvia Park, the new six-level medical office development at 3 Te Kehu Way is advancing with similar momentum. The building's exterior is now complete, with its innovative and distinctive design already becoming a prominent feature on the Mt Wellington landscape. Internal fitouts are now underway at 3 Te Kehu Way and is on track to be completed in the first quarter of 2023, marking a next step towards the creation of a thriving commercial precinct at Sylvia Park. Around two-thirds of 3 Te Kehu Way's net lettable area is either committed or subject to advanced negotiations, with an impressive lineup of tenants in place, including Tamaki Health, Horizon Radiology, Geneva Finance, and co-working operator, IWG. In addition, the redevelopment of Sylvia Lane was recently finished, creating an exciting new all-weather dining precinct. Sylvia Lane is set to become a cornerstone of the center's entertainment offering, providing an attractive place for people to eat, drink, and socialize. The enhancement of Sylvia Lane is expected to drive [customer and chain] demand, helping to generate sales, and ultimately, rental growth. In early November, Kiwi Property's Drury Private Plan Change was approved by the Environment Court, confirming our landholding as the site for the future metropolitan Town Centre. Stage one earthworks are now underway Drury, marking the next step in Kiwi Property's ambition to create a six Green Star, transit-oriented community south of Auckland. The earthworks are expected to take two years at a cost of around $30 million. Pleasingly, the [upzoning] of our [Drury Site] has already delivered valuation gains, with the landholding now worth more than double the purchase price. And expected to increase further once earth and civil works are complete. With the Private Plan Change now secured, we've also resumed the Fast-track consenting process with the goal of accelerating resource consent and facilitating the creation of 13 residential super-lots. The potential sale of these super-lots will enable us to realize returns from the project and assist with future funding. The disposal of non-core properties and subsequent recycling of capital is a central pillar of our funding strategy. And we've made important strides on this front in the six months to 30 September. Today, we announce the unconditional sale of 44 The Terrace in Wellington for $48 million, with $2 million retained for seismic costs. The transaction is expected to settle on December 15, 2022. And delivers a property level IRR of 12.2% from inception. Westgate Lifestyle has also now been listed for sale, following the disposal of Northlands Shopping Centre in Christchurch for $151 million, net of seismic costs, which is due to settle on November 30, 2022. The proceeds raised from these transactions will be used to repay debt and fund our development pipeline, delivering what we believe will be better long-term value for shareholders. One of our business' strengths is its large strategic landholding, including more than 125 hectares across our mixed-use assets at Sylvia Park, LynnMall, The Base, and Drury. This landholding provides an extensive range of options and provides the flexibility to dictate the timing and speed of our development activities. We currently have around $217 million of development expenditure remaining at 3 Te Kehu Way and Sylvia Park build-to-rent. We are proactively managing pricing and expect both projects to maintain the target yields that were previously disclosed to the market. While these developments and the stage one earthworks at Drury present exciting opportunities for Kiwi Property, we'll maintain a cautious approach to the timing of further activity. New developments will only occur when market conditions, cost, and return metrics are acceptable. Our priority is to ensure the right financial conditions and suitable funding are in place before any further construction projects begin. So, we're making the best use of shareholder capital. Kiwi Property posted a strong operational result in the first half of the FY2023 financial year, delivering growth in key metrics such as sales, rental income, operating profit, and adjusted funds from operations. As I've already mentioned, net rental income rose to a record high of a $100 million, up 6.3% on the same time last year, driven by sustained revenue uplift at Sylvia Park in particular. Operating profit before tax was also up, increasing 4.2% to $65.1 million, reflecting the pleasing performance of our diversified asset portfolio. AFFO rose 35.8% to $65.2 million, assisted by the release of COVID-19 rental abatement accruals, which were not required. The company's robust operational result was unfortunately unable to offset the impact of rising interest rates and the global softening of capitalization rates. As a result of these headwinds, the fair value of Kiwi Property investment portfolio declined by an unrealized 5.8% or $213.3 million, causing the business to post a net loss after tax of $151.1 million. While the decrease in fair value of our property portfolio and subsequent impact on net profit is disappointing, it's not unexpected given the well-documented challenges facing the global economy. By actively managing our assets and tightly controlling our cost [base], we'll be in the strongest position to maximize asset vaues going forward. The company continue to drive strong rental growth during the period, including a 4.9% increase in new leases and rent reviews across our office and mixed-use portfolio. Our ability to increase rents while simultaneously securing a pipeline of new tenants is a testament to the demand for space in our assets, led by Sylvia Park, LynnMall, and The Base. This demand enabled our portfolio to remain almost fully occupied at 30 September and achieve a robust weighted average lease expiry of 4.6 years. Retail sales continue to bounce back strongly post COVID-19 with reduced Auckland lockdowns, enabling stores to trade for 13 more days than they did in the preceding 12 months. Total sales were $1.51 billion on an [MAT] basis, up around $280 million on the prior comparable period, a very good outcome considering cost of living pressures currently facing Kiwi consumers. Total sales growth was an impressive 9.6% on the prior year across our mixed-use and large format retail centers combined. While specialty sales at our mixed-use shopping centers increased to $12,900 a square meter, specialty gross occupancy costs were 12.1%, a favorable position compared to many Australasian REITs, highlighting the highly productive and well-placed nature of our retail tenancies. Kiwi Property undertook several capital management activities in the first half of the financial year, including increasing our bank debt facilities from $850 million to $950 million. Post the reporting period, our bank debt facilities were increased to $1 billion, and the weighted average term of all debt facilities was extended to 4.1 years. In line with most of our listed property peers, we have also granted mortgage security in respect of our properties and increased our bank gearing covenant to 50%. The weighted average cost of debt grew from 3.85% to 4.41%, driven by the increase in interest rates that have been a recent feature of the international and domestic economies. Maintaining a robust and flexible balance sheet is a priority for the business in the current market. The previously mentioned unrealized reduction in the fair value of our property portfolio, so our gearing increased to 35.7% as at September 30, 2022. Net asset backing per share was similarly affected, decreasing to $1.31 per share. It's important to note, however, that once our gearing figures adjusted on a pro-forma basis to reflect the settlement of Northlands on 30 November and 44 The Terrace on 15 December, pro-forma gearing decreases to approximately 32%. Kiwi Property will pay a quarterly cash dividend of $0.01425 per share, taking year-to-date interim cash dividend to $0.0285 per share, up almost 4% on the prior period. Today, we are pleased to confirm our full year dividend guidance at $0.057 per share, representing a gross dividend yield of 9.3% based on the current share price and assuming a 33% personal tax rate while enabling us to retain earnings to fund growth. As always, it's important to note that the payment of any further dividends is contingent on the performance of the company through the remainder of the 2023 financial year and barring material adverse effects or unforeseen circumstances. As you have seen, Kiwi Property delivered a strong operating result in the first half of the 2023 financial year and took important steps forward in the delivery of our strategy. As we head into the second half of the financial year, we have four specific priorities. First, we'll strive to maintain balance sheet flexibility and capacity through a combination of cost control, capital recycling, and strict financial discipline. Second, we'll advance to stage one earthworks at Drury and move forward with the Fast-track application, taking us closer to having the option of selling down super-lots in order to release capital. Third, we'll continue pushing forward with a dedicated leasing program at 3 Te Kehu Way, with the aim of having all tenancies committed in time for opening. column4: Newell Brands' (NASDAQ:NWL) Dividend Will Be $0.23
column10: [Newell Brands Inc. (NASDAQ:NWL) will pay a dividend of $0.23 on the 15th of December. This means the annual payment is 7.0% of the current stock price, which is above the average for the industry.While the dividend yield is important for income investors, it is also important to consider any large share price moves, as this will generally outweigh any gains from distributions. Newell Brands' stock price has reduced by 37% in the last 3 months, which is not ideal for investors and can explain a sharp increase in the dividend yield. View our latest analysis for Newell Brands Newell Brands' Payment Has Solid Earnings CoverageWhile it is great to have a strong dividend yield, we should also consider whether the payment is sustainable. Prior to this announcement, Newell Brands' earnings easily covered the dividend, but free cash flows were negative. No cash flows could definitely make returning cash to shareholders difficult, or at least mean the balance sheet will come under pressure.Looking forward, earnings per share is forecast to rise by 48.7% over the next year. If the dividend continues on this path, the payout ratio could be 47% by next year, which we think can be pretty sustainable going forward.historic-dividendNewell Brands Has A Solid Track RecordThe company has a sustained record of paying dividends with very little fluctuation. Since 2012, the annual payment back then was $0.32, compared to the most recent full-year payment of $0.92. This works out to be a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 11% a year over that time. We can see that payments have shown some very nice upward momentum without faltering, which provides some reassurance that future payments will also be reliable.Newell Brands May Find It Hard To Grow The DividendInvestors could be attracted to the stock based on the quality of its payment history. Let's not jump to conclusions as things might not be as good as they appear on the surface. In the last five years, Newell Brands' earnings per share has shrunk at approximately 4.5% per annum. Declining earnings will inevitably lead to the company paying a lower dividend in line with lower profits. Earnings are forecast to grow over the next 12 months and if that happens we could still be a little bit cautious until it becomes a pattern.Story continuesIn SummaryOverall, we don't think this company makes a great dividend stock, even though the dividend wasn't cut this year. While the low payout ratio is a redeeming feature, this is offset by the minimal cash to cover the payments. We would be a touch cautious of relying on this stock primarily for the dividend income.It's important to note that companies having a consistent dividend policy will generate greater investor confidence than those having an erratic one. Meanwhile, despite the importance of dividend payments, they are not the only factors our readers should know when assessing a company. column4: PaperMate® Launches the "Thanks to Teachers" Initiative, Supporting Teachers Nationwide
column10: [PaperMate® is donating $100,000 to the Kids In Need Foundation and its Supply a Teacher ProgramATLANTA, Nov. 17, 2022 /PRNewswire/ --  PaperMate® , part of the Newell Brands global portfolio of brands, knows that America's next stories are being written by today's students, and teachers are the ones helping to shape them. In fact, according to Education Week, the average teacher influences over 3,000 students and families throughout their careers. That's why, PaperMate is launching the "Thanks to Teachers" initiative.While Teacher Appreciation Week has become synonymous with showing thanks and admiration for teachers across the nation, PaperMate is encouraging the 87 percent of people who wished they had told their best teachers how much they appreciated their efforts, according to an ING Survey, to stand together and thank the teachers in their lives that helped shape their (or their children's) future, year-round. As part of the "Thanks to Teachers" initiative, PaperMate is encouraging everyone to write thank you notes and post on Instagram using the hashtags #ThankstoTeachers and tagging @PaperMate to have a chance to be featured on the brand's Instagram."Teachers dedicate their lives to helping educate and raise our future generations – it's time we start prioritizing and showing teachers the support, recognition, and appreciation, they deserve. As we head into the new year, PaperMate is committed to supporting teachers across the nation who build our future and form our youth," said Kris Malkoski, CEO, Writing Business Unit at Newell Brands.In spirit of giving thanks, PaperMate is also donating school supplies and $100,000 to the Kids In Need Foundation's Supply A Teacher Program, to help eliminate the burden teachers face by purchasing supplies out of their own pocket. According to Kids In Need Foundation's annual teacher survey, as teachers prepare for the second half of the school year, 91 percent don't have the supplies they need to start the second semester of the school year in January. The donations will help supply under-resourced teachers and their students with essential supplies they need to fuel a full semester of active learning including pens, pencils, markers, and so much more.Story continuesFor those looking to make a donation to teachers in their community, please visit (https://www.kinf.org/papermate/) to help supply teachers in the Kids In Need Foundation Supply A Teacher Program.For more information about PaperMate products, please visit https://www.papermate.com/.About Newell Brands  Newell Brands (NASDAQ: NWL) is a leading global consumer goods company with a strong portfolio of well-known brands, including Rubbermaid, FoodSaver, Calphalon, Sistema, Sharpie, PaperMate, Dymo, EXPO, Elmer's, Yankee Candle, Graco, NUK, Rubbermaid Commercial Products, Spontex, Coleman, Campingaz, Oster, Sunbeam and Mr. Coffee. (Operator Instructions) I would now like to hand the call over to CEO, Jeremy Nicoll. Please go ahead. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [2] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us on the first-half call for Arvida. I'm pleased to report a very solid set of numbers for the first-half of FY '23. We saw our net profit-after-tax on a IFRS basis of $89 million, which was up 18% on the prior corresponding period. Our key metric of underlying profit was up 46% on the prior corresponding period, to $38.9 million. On an EPS basis, that's up 10% to $0.054 cents per share. Obviously, the first-half that we are reporting, does include a contribution from the Arena villages that we bought in November last year. Operating cash flow was up to $77.4 million, and importantly, our gearing remained towards the lower end of our target range, at 28%, through our stated ranges between 25% to 35%, so very considerably geared going into the next calendar year. Subsequent to the end of the reporting period, we did receive a further $24 million from the sale of a piece of residual land from Waikanae Beach. We settled Waikanae Beach early in the half, and then sold the ramp off and received that money post that offset. During the period, we did refinance our banking syndicate, added $50 million with the limits, and also extended the maturities of those. Very pleased that ANZ and BNZ were very supportive of Arvida and its activities. The real highlight came through from the sales activities, with the total value of our sales up 31% to $168 million. This included $28 million worth of gains from resales at a higher margin of 30%. Development gains also increased, up to just under $15 million at a higher margin of 20%. We did have some impacts through COVID over the period. Obviously, at the start of the period, with sort of the peak of the Omicron pandemic. So during that period, we did restrict admissions to our care facility, and we also incurred higher operating costs through that period. As a result, material occupancy for the half was at 88%, that has rebounded to 90% at September, and has continued to improve to now being at 92%. We have seen the value of our assets increase to $3.6 billion, that's on the back of the development activity going on through the portfolio and also the increase in the valuation of our investment properties of $89 million. NTA per share increased to $1.93, and the embedded value per share increased to $1.53. Based on current trading, we're trading at about $1.30 as of now, so still a significant discount to both of those 2 metrics. On our construction business, we delivered 51 new units during the half, and we are on target to deliver another 219 in the second-half, and I'll talk about those in a bit more detail coming through. We did add 1 further the greenfield site to the portfolio, in Lincoln, in Greater Christchurch and we have 2 sites under conditional contract. On the following page, you can see the increase in our key metrics around revenue up 16%, underlying profit up 46% and then operating cash flow up 12% to $77 million. In terms of strategy, the most important thing is our people and that's both our resident community and also our team members. It's been a pretty challenging period that we've been dealing with over the last 6 months. So at this stage, just like to thank all of our team members for the huge amount of business and work that they've put in over the period and, also to our resident body for helping us work our way through that pandemic earlier in the year. Moving on to some of the development activity, these are lovely shots of Te Puna Waiora and Kerikeri. You can see the progress there that we're making with that development. During the period, we delivered 9 villas up there, with an average value of $920,000, and recently we've been hitting new highs in terms of sales pricing on the next stage of villas that are under construction up there. We saw a pretty solid level of pricing in place, particularly at some of the premium sites, and places like Te Puna Waiora and Waimea Plains, which are our first 2 greenfield development, selling down extremely well. In the second half of the year, we will deliver 219 and 2 of those projects kind of complete right at the end of the financial year, that's Lauriston Park, which is a 63 care suite, and Aria Bay, which has 57 independent apartments. New inventory levels were less than 2%, and that also includes our care suites that we delivered at Rhodes on Cashmere during the period. With the sort of economic outlook for the next year set to weaken, we have retained our build rate target for FY '24 at 250 plus units, and our development mix does allow us to flex on villa builds, if demand slows. But at this stage and we are seeing record levels of demand. On the next couple of pages, we can see some of the projects that we have completed during the period. And also on page 8, some of the developments in progress. As you can see our Aria Bay is well progressed, as is Lauriston Park. Peninsula Club, new apartments, we finished in this quarter and the final stages of villas at Bethlehem shows continued at pace, with a great level of demand. The kids and apartment building at Queenstown is now coming out of the ground, and you can see the picture there on slide 8. In terms of our greenfield developments, we've outlined the 5 different greenfield communities that we have, with the units still to be delivered, as shown in the table. As I mentioned, we have added the Lincoln site at the 11 hectare sites and the aim there is to deliver 200 and 50 care suites. On page 10 is a beautiful picture of a green paddock which is Lincoln. It is well located within a new subdivision at [sites] and the vendor has an ongoing rezoning obligation over the next 12 months. In terms of our overall development pipeline, the pipeline has increased to just over 2,100 units, which gives us plenty of scope and pleasingly, you can see now that that greenfield component of the pipeline, is roughly half of our overall pipeline and without closing out some of our other brownfield development opportunities that we've had within the portfolio. At this point, we'll just hand over to Mark Wells, our Chief Financial Officer to run through the financial picture. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Mark Wells, Arvida Group Limited - CFO [3] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Good morning, everybody. Net profit for the period was $89.2 million, but the key driver being the fair value increase of $89 million, an increase of $0.29. Revenue grew 16%, with the contribution of the Arena Villages. The additional operations increased operating expenses to $104 million, with higher COVID and employee costs included in the period. Care revenue was at $58 million on lower care occupancy and divestments. Occupancy in the previous year -- occupancy is improving and the 5.5% funding increase applied from 1st of September 2022. Village revenue increased, reflecting the Arena and also the increased development. On to ORA resales, resales were 164 units, up a pleasing 23% on the previous period. There were $28.3 million resale gains, with increased margins of 30% on the back of a pricing increase of 6%. Over the page shows another strong increase in the embedded value to $1.1 billion, representing $1.53 per share. This is on the back of increased pricing. And on the lower right hand side, the affordability graph shows a buffer still in place between house prices and our unit pricing. The new unit ORA sale -- the period at -- the period was strong with new unit sales gains up to $14.9 million on a margin of 20%. The underlying profit increased to $38.9 million for the period, up 46% on first-half 2022 -- '21, with Arena villages contributing $16 million. Annuity EBITDA increased 52% to $34 million. In terms of the balance sheet, total assets are now at $3.6 billion, with strong development pushing up the investment property to $3.3 billion. On to the capital structure; drawn debt is at $555 million on increased development completions in the second half. In the period, refinance was completed to extend tenures, and additional $50 million added limit to the facility. The gearing was at 28% and the loan-to-value ratio at 31%, being low for the sector. Interest cover was 2.3 times on our general facility, that includes all of the interest. We are in discussions with our banks to remove one technicality in the calculation, and if applied retrospectively, the calculation would be at 3.1 times. Cash flows -- on operating cash flows, this was up to $77 million and increased 12% on increased operations. Strategy and outlook, I'll just pass back to Jeremy Nicoll to continue. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [4] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So on the ageing population slide, there is a huge amount of inherent growth within the sector over the next 20, 40 years. So what we're seeing at the moment is very, very strong levels of demand for our product, and this was reflected in our ability to increase the sales prices over the 6 month period. So when you look at all the resales that we completed in the 6 months, on average, but pricing that we achieved was 6% higher than the independent value assist at 31 March, 2022. We've also been able to increase the prices of the ex-Arena villages by just over 10% since acquisition, which has created increases in both the investment value, but also our resale gain line. On strategy, and our direction remains the same. We do want to continue to transform the ageing experience for older New Zealanders. We have an aim to reach 50 retirement communities of scale, that still offer a continuum of care. One of the key things that we have been working on, is how we engage with our people and making Arvida the best place to work in the sector. We've also been very, very focused on how our residents in our communities are treated, and how they're feeling. We're just launching our annual resident survey at the moment, so we'll be able to publish the results of that satisfaction outcome early in the New Year. On the sustainability perspective, we are hitting well ahead of the curve. Recently, Standard and Poor's raised it up in the top quartile globally for our sustainability initiatives. Toitu recently completed the audit of our FY '22 emissions, and on an intensity basis, we are moving well towards our target of reducing them by 20% up to FY '25. In terms of the outlook, there has been a number of issues that the team have been facing in the first half and some of those issues will continue, as we move into the calendar year of 2023. To reflect that, we will retain our annual build rate target at 250 plus, instead of moving it up to 300 as previously indicated. We have the lowest gearing in the sector, and we have a continued preference of villa led [broad] acre development. On the care side of our business, the government funding for care continues to lag the cost to deliberate. We are very pleased that the government made an announcement yesterday, and intends to fund pay parity for nurses in aged care, the details of which are yet to be agreed and finalized, but that work will be led by the NZACA, our (inaudible) body with (inaudible) the Ministry of Health early in the New Year. The government indicated they'll provide $40 million of additional funding through to 30th June, 2023 and from 1 July, 2023 onwards, there was a commitment for a further $200 million worth of funding for nurses. Look, this is a great start, but it does not completely solve the cost of care delivery. It deals with one aspect, which is nurse pay parity with the public system. So there will be continued work from this sector on restoring profitability to enable continued investment into the sector. There have been some changes to immigration policy, that have started to address some of the resourcing debt. But our view has been very, very clear, and that nurses should have an immediate pathway to residency in New Zealand, and the current immigration settings are hampering nurses coming into the country. We are still committed to the continuum of care, based on the current profitability of care. The development at this stage and the future will be all through care suite products, either new or retrofitted where we can. We do want to keep working with the government, as I talked about before about care funding, to enable continued investment into the sector, to help all New Zealanders, when they reach older years, so that they can all get the care that they deserve. In terms of the 1H dividend, we've retained the dividend at the same level as the prior half, at $0.025 per share. There is no imputation credits or supplementary dividend payable to non-residents. We have suspended the dividend reinvestment plan for this dividend payment, given the discount-to-value that we are trading at, and we will actively review this again at the final result. At this point, I'll pause and we'll hand over for questions. ================================================================================ Questions and Answers -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [1] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (Operator Instructions) Our first question comes from the line of Bianca Fledderus of UBS. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bianca Fledderus, UBS Investment Bank, Research Division - Analyst [2] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So firstly I was just wondering what's the reason if you suspended the DRP for this dividend payment? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [3] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Speaking for the [future] is just the level of the share price compared to asset backing. It was a hotly discussed topic on the agenda for the Board. And on-balance, the Board decided that, given where the stock price was trading, that the dividend reinvestment plan would be suspended. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bianca Fledderus, UBS Investment Bank, Research Division - Analyst [4] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. Great. And then just on your balance sheet. So gearing ratio, I guess looks fine at 28%. But yet your interest cover does look quite tight. Since -- I appreciate you mentioned before that you are talking to the bank about this. But how confident are you that this calculation will change? And if not, then will that limit your developments going forward? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [5] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Look, we are very confident. And I probably can't say much more than that, but yes, very confident that it will be resolved. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bianca Fledderus, UBS Investment Bank, Research Division - Analyst [6] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. And so with regards to your deliveries for the second-half being 219 units, you are confident as well that you can achieve that? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [7] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so of the 219, is the 120 at 2 major projects, Lauriston and Aria Bay. Lauriston is really well progressed, that will probably be completed in February, start of March. And Aria Bay is progressing really well, so that will be complete towards the end of March. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Bianca Fledderus, UBS Investment Bank, Research Division - Analyst [8] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. And then just with regards to the current environment, are you doing any sort of promotions like no fees for a year, anything like that, just to try and attract new residents to your villages? Do you have to do stuff like that, or is it still just solid demand for that, I think to pull those levers? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [9] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So at the moment, there is significant level of demand. So we don't -- we're not running any above-the-line promotions at any sites. The demand is there. They just need to work-through the health sale process, and in some cases, the people's houses are taking a little bit longer to settle, and that will give them a bit more of a grace period to get through that. And our balance sheet, we will disclose the level of residents advances, and (technical difficulty) buyback about $2 million over the 6 months. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [10] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Our next question comes from the line of Andrew Steele of Jarden. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Andrew Steele, Jarden Limited, Research Division - Director of Equity Research [11] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The first one from me is, on the current I guess momentum in the business. How things changed, if at all since the trading update at the beginning of October? Is the cost run rate consistent, and is your sales outlook consistent with that update? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [12] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so sales momentum is still really, really strong. Probably September was our best month of the year, in terms of sales settlement and that momentum continues into the trading that we've seen in October and November. In terms of the care side of the business, we described the occupancy, which is the key factor. So revenues increasing, as Mark pointed out, the 5.5% increase in care fees was only effective from 1 September. So we'll see the benefit of that number coming through. As you recall, the government thought, it was good to offer 3% increase in our fees from 1 July, and as we disagreed with that, they only paid us a portion of it, for the 1st of July and August. So only a small amount of the increase within the first-half numbers. So you'll see that increase starting to come through in the second half as with previous outbreaks, we have paid our people more to work through those outbreaks. So that really impacted sort of April, May, June, and things are starting to normalize on the loss of hours and employment cost basis. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Andrew Steele, Jarden Limited, Research Division - Director of Equity Research [13] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- All right. And just following on from your comments on sales momentum, could you talk to how margins have been progressing as well post downsizing the start the second half for both new sale margin and retail margin versus 1H? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [14] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so just consistent with first-half really. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Andrew Steele, Jarden Limited, Research Division - Director of Equity Research [15] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- And whilst I appreciate the details are yet to be ironed out on nurse pay parity settlement, I assume you've done some sort of rough workings on it. Do you have a rough sense as to the potential uplift you might get from it? And do you have a sense as to what that might mean for Improved operational efficiency? Or I guess, another way of putting it, reduced staff turnover, as a result of pay parity? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [16] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. So you've got the same information as I do, on what the government has announced. I don't have any further information. They're talking about $200 million to pay 20,000 nurses, and that's $10,000 a pop, assuming that they are all full-time workers. We currently employ about 250 nurses, so it was $10,000 a pop, that's $2.5 million. So that's kind of the rough order of magnitude. And then, I forgot the second half of your question, sorry? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Andrew Steele, Jarden Limited, Research Division - Director of Equity Research [17] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, it was just on the assumption about that you've done a pay parity of higher staff turnover, assuming it results in low staff turnover, do you have a sense to what impact that might have in terms of improved efficiency on the business? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [18] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so if you look at the NZACA Annual Report for -- that was published a few months back, they had the sector turnover for registered nurses at a 48% level. So that gives you an indication of the turnover that the sector is dealing with. Pay parity will go long way towards helping that. But the devil will be in the details, so we do need to keep on working with the government, to iron out the details of how that's going to work. I know there's more pay settlements happening with the public system, what's the implication there. So there is a lot still to be worked through to sort of get a real handle on it. But it's a great first step, we've been asking and talking about it with the government for a number of years now. So it's great that they've finally drawn a line in the sands, but we still need to work through the detail. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Andrew Steele, Jarden Limited, Research Division - Director of Equity Research [19] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- And just a last one from me is on how you're thinking about acquisitions at the moment. Given where your share price is relative to NTA, how are you thinking about the prospects for potential M&A? And assuming that that's going to be somewhat difficult, if you were to do a larger transaction? What's the necessary run rate of greenfield land acquisitions that you need per annum, to meet current and medium-term development guidance? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [20] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so we -- yes, obviously, M&A activity at the moment is particularly constrained, given where our share price is. So we've been trading at a 30% to 40% discount to valuation, buying up, big assets or a group of assets and shaving 30% to 40% off the value of them on day 1, isn't particularly appealing for anybody. So as you've seen, we've -- we have not bought anything since November last year, when the share price was in excess of $2. There's been a number of -- in a couple of public announced portfolios were up for sale. Obviously, we wouldn't be able to complete, though there has been a number of single assets that come across our desk. And again there's not really much point spending much time on them at that point. So we have really pivoted towards the greenfield land strategy. Never say never on (inaudible) acquisitions, but at this point in time, it's not on the radar, and we'd be looking to continue with what we have been doing in the last little while, of trying to look at about 2 different sites or 3 sites per annum of greenfield land. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [21] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Our next question comes from the line of Nick Mar of Macquarie. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nick Mar, Macquarie Research - Analyst [22] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Just following on the nurse question. Where is your pay relative to the DHB rates. And do you have any thoughts on that comments in one of the articles about how those already paying DHB rates wouldn't be eligible funding? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [23] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I can't disclose our nurse rates. The comment is one of the details that needs to be worked through. My expectation is that, there will be an increase to the current funding rates, to a level of care to reflect pay parity to nurses, and there'll be some sort of similar mechanism that they've used for caregivers, where there's different grades and minimum rates payable to those different grades. So that's my understanding of how we will pay them out, and in that situation, those big rates would be deployed consistently across the country. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nick Mar, Macquarie Research - Analyst [24] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. I guess, just asking maybe in a slight different way, especially as you did get to the $2.5 million you estimated before. How much do you think you can hold on to versus having to pass-through? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [25] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I can't talk about that on this call. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nick Mar, Macquarie Research - Analyst [26] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay, that's fine. And then just kind of clarity, in terms of the outlook commentary, it's been a little bit confusing from the initial guidance to the update to now. When you talk about the sort of dividends being consistent, are you now at $0.055, or was it still the $0.06, i.e. annualizing the second-half '22 number, which was the original outlook, and from what I understand, the number that you used at the investor update in our portfolio? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [27] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, so if you're looking at it, I think about the base case being the same as FY '22, so that's $0.055 per share. We want to be targeting at the midpoint, or maybe slightly below it. And if we can, we'll look to increase that second-half dividend as well that, there's a lot to play out in the second-half before we provide anything more definitive than just looking at the same level as last year. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nick Mar, Macquarie Research - Analyst [28] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. And is it correct that essentially, at the sort of investor update, it was $0.06 at the midpoint, which was $0.12 of earnings and now it would be $0.055 somewhere around there, 50% which could be sort of in that $0.11 to $0.115 range, is that a fair way of thinking about it now? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [29] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. I think the fair way to think about it, is the same as last year. And if things go well, there may be some upside on the dividend. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [30] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Next question comes from the line of Aaron Ibbotson of Forsyth Barr. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Aaron Ibbotson, Forsyth Barr Group Ltd., Research Division - Research Analyst [31] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Just a couple of quick ones for me, as you've touched on most of it. But firstly, I'm just curious to hear your thoughts around what I thought was a sensible reduction in build rate ambitions for at least FY '24. And I guess my question is more broadly in light of how the market is pricing your stock and the movements in debt and interest rate markets. How do you think about this 25% to 35% gearing target? Is there a case to be made that it could be a little bit lower, is that how I should interpret your sort of slightly reduction in build rate? And more generally, how you're thinking about capital allocation, when it comes to newbuild versus either paying down debt or even buying back some shares at these levels? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [32] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes. So we have made that decision just to keep the build rate at the same level of 250 plus. We do want to be able to have a good mix of what we're building between villas, which are a little bit quicker to recycle the cash, than care apartment buildings, which may take a bit longer. We are cognizant that no one knows what the economic environment in the next calendar year is going to be. So we're very pleased to be going into that period with the lowest gearing in the sector. 28% is a good starting point for us. We do want to keep building through-the-cycle. We do see that, as talked about earlier on, there is strong levels of demand. We are more of a growth stock than a dividend reliant stock. So for us, continuing to invest in our business, makes sense. Obviously, we have talked about share buybacks as an organization, and decided that at this point in time, we'd rather keep our gearing rates at the lower level, to enable us to continue to build through the cycle. So capital management is a key focus for us, as we speak, with those rising interest rates. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Aaron Ibbotson, Forsyth Barr Group Ltd., Research Division - Research Analyst [33] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thank you and apologies to come back to the question around, sort of what I guess is a convoluted earnings guidance through the dividend payout ratio. But I didn't pick up any change in language from this slide 26 versus your update from September, is there a change? Because I read it as being the same message as you gave in September. But your answer to the previous question suggested to me, that there had been a slight down adjustment. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [34] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- So it's just interpretation. So effectively what the slide said, that the dividend for this payout for the full year is likely to be towards the midpoint of payout range. So that's -- in plain language, midpoints -- just being -- it's going to be towards that, which means that it will be -- hopefully in the 40s, but at the high side of 40s, and that we looking at the base case to retain the full year dividend at the same level as FY '22. So it's $0.055 a share. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Aaron Ibbotson, Forsyth Barr Group Ltd., Research Division - Research Analyst [35] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Okay. That is sort of what you said in this September update. But I guess, the reason we interpreted that as being $0.06 or the message around it was, more than 2 times 3, than the $0.055. But okay, that is then clear. Thank you very much. Maybe, I am just going to throw it out there, a question on sort of general OpEx and inflationary wage pressures. What are you experiencing at the moment around wages, if we ignore nurses for now, and other costs, should we expect sort of continued sort of mid-single-digit OpEx growth half-on-half, or is it tapering off a little bit? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Mark Wells, Arvida Group Limited - CFO [36] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Hey Aaron, I would expect similar rates at this stage. Certainly in terms of general costs, they are being passed through to everybody. And you're right, there is still pressure in those employee type areas, as we know, it's carrying on at least through to the end of this year and probably through to 31 March, by the looks of things. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [37] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (Operator Instructions) Our next question comes from the line of Shane Solly of Harbour Asset. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Shane Solly, Harbour Asset Management Limited - Director & Portfolio Manager [38] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Firstly, congrats on navigating another -- through a tough half and to your team doing a great job. And also to acknowledge your leading the charge and making people aware of this funding issue that's in here. My question, just in terms of the settlement -- questions in terms of delays, and you had a great chat on sustainable affordability. Can you talk about whether you are seeing much of a gap between the sales and the sales process, or whatnot, and what you might do to address that? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [39] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, we would -- it's definitely been a half of -- 2 halves casting back to the first quarter, they were -- it was in the middle of a pandemic, and it was a bit more uncertainty that where house prices were going and where interest rates were going. So we did have a lower level of settlements than we expected in that first quarter. In the second quarter, things just ramped back up to where they should be, and even exceeded where we thought. So it definitely did change sort of midway through the first half and we're now at the point where most people know where the house prices are, most people know where interest rates are. There's been some [tightening] out in the lending rules. So we are much more in a period of equilibrium. We're not really seeing a lot of issues, but some people are having trouble selling the house. There's no doubt about that. But that's something that we just worked through, with the resident and we're just going to be on top of it, so we need to know with business houses, what the value is, who is doing the sale or what is the process, what are the timelines, and just working with the prospective residents to help them navigate that, so we can get the right outcome. But we also need to be cognizant that if someone is not going to complete, we need to move on to someone else, because there is enough demand for us to sell the product, we just got to make sure that we're working with our prospects and our databases and that we're trying to give the right results for everyone. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Shane Solly, Harbour Asset Management Limited - Director & Portfolio Manager [40] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Great, thank you, Jeremy. Really appreciate it. Thank you. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [41] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Yes, thanks for your comments too Shane. It has been a very, very tough period for the team, and they've done an awesome job through this period. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [42] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thank you. At this time, I'd like to turn the call back over to Jeremy Nicoll for any closing remarks. Sir? -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Jeremy Nicoll, Arvida Group Limited - CEO [43] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thank you very much for your time on the call today. I think Arvida is in a very, very strong position as we move into the second half, for a period of improved performance over what was a very good first half to the year. Thank you to everyone on the call for your support of Arvida. It is really appreciated and we hope if I don't see you before Christmas, you will have a great holiday. I think everyone deserves that after this year. Thank you. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Operator [44] -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.]
